text.hook:
Rule of 3, Rule of 5, Rule of 0.
Everyone can name them. Few can say what the compiler actually generates.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 💡
text.body:
Inside:
1. Constructor or assignment, copy or move
2. What declaring one member does to the others
3. A correct copy assignment, and copy-and-swap
4. Writing the moves, and members that block them
5. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: Special members, what the compiler generates, and what it costs to get wrong.

slides.title: Two questions pick the special member

cards.label: Does the destination exist?
cards.text: No: a **constructor**. Yes: an **assignment**. `T b = a;` is initialization: copy constructor.

cards.label: What is the source?
cards.text: An lvalue: **copy**. An rvalue (`std::move(a)`, a temporary): **move**.

slides.takeaway: The compiler writes them memberwise. Wrong exactly when a member is a raw handle: a pointer, a file descriptor.

slides.title: What declaring one member does
slides.takeaway: Not declared: rvalues fall back to the copy. Deleted: the call does not compile.

slides.title: A correct copy assignment, in order
steps: Survive self-assignment: `a = a` must not free the source first
Allocate and copy **before** deleting (a throwing `new` leaves `*this` unchanged)

slides.title: Copy into a temporary, then swap

cards.label: How
cards.text: `Buffer tmp(other); swap(*this, tmp);` The destructor of `tmp` frees the **old** resource.

cards.label: Gains
cards.text: Strong exception guarantee and self-assignment safety, no branch.

cards.label: Cost
cards.text: Always allocates. A hand-written version can reuse capacity.

slides.title: Writing the moves
items: Steal, then reset the source: `data_(std::exchange(o.data_, nullptr))`
The moved-from destructor still runs: without the reset, double delete
Move assignment releases its old resource. It does not allocate
Guard self-move, and mark both moves `noexcept`

slides.title: One member changes the whole class
slides.takeaway: A `const` member still allows `push_back`, but `std::sort` and `erase` fail to compile: they assign.

items.myth: "`T b = a;` calls the assignment operator."
items.truth: It is initialization: the copy constructor.

items.myth: "I wrote a move constructor, I still get the default copy assignment."
items.truth: Both copy operations become deleted. `b = a;` does not compile.
It is UB. It may seem to work, corrupt the heap, or crash much later.

items.myth: "Move assignment needs a temporary in case allocation throws."
items.truth: Move assignment does not allocate. That concern belongs to copy assignment.

items.myth: "The default move of a raw pointer member transfers ownership."
items.truth: It copies the pointer and leaves the source unchanged. Only your code can null it.

items.myth: "Every class with a destructor needs five hand-written bodies."
items.truth: It needs all five **decided**: some are `= default` or `= delete`.

slides.hero:
Wrote a destructor?
Decide what copy
and move mean.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The class frees its buffer in the destructor.
The program only prints the size. What can go wrong?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: No assignment, no move, no explicit copy anywhere in main. Look at the parameter.

slides.title: What happens?

slides.verdict_sub: glibc: "free(): double free detected in tcache 2", abort
bullets: Pass by value calls the **implicit copy constructor**: `b` shares `a`'s array.
`print` returns: `~b` frees the array. End of `main`: `~a` frees it again.

slides.title: Decide what a copy means
slides.tip: Rule of 0: hold a `std::vector<int>` and write none of this.
slides.takeaway: A user destructor without copy control is a time bomb. Every hidden copy arms it.

text.hook:
The class has a perfectly good move constructor.
The vector grows twice. What does it print?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: "Why is my vector copying?" Cause number one, in 15 lines.

slides.title: GCC/libstdc++. What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Cause: the move constructor is not `noexcept`
bullets: `emplace_back` builds the new element in place: nothing printed for it.
libstdc++ grows capacity 1 ➜ 2 ➜ 4: relocates one element, then two.
To keep the strong guarantee, vector uses `std::move_if_noexcept`.
Move may throw and a copy exists: it **copies**.
slides.wrong: "`| move | move move |`: it has a move constructor"

slides.title: One keyword
slides.tip: Same symptom, other cause: a user-declared destructor removes the implicit move entirely.
slides.takeaway: A move constructor that is not `noexcept` is ignored by vector growth whenever copying is possible.

text.hook:
No destructor. No copy constructor. No move constructor.
The class owns a heap buffer.
So copying it must be broken. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The best way to follow the Rule of 5 is to write none of them.

slides.title: No special members written. What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Deep copy and a `noexcept` move, both for free
bullets: The implicit copy calls `vector`'s copy: separate storage, so `b.data[0] = 7` never touches `a`.
The implicit move calls `vector`'s move: O(1) buffer transfer, `noexcept`.
The implicit destructor frees the buffer. All five are correct, none written.
Add a member later: the implicit functions pick it up. Hand-written ones silently skip it.

slides.title: Pick the member type by the semantics you want
slides.code:
std::vector<int> v;        // deep copy
std::unique_ptr<int[]> p;  // move-only
std::shared_ptr<int[]> s;  // shared
slides.tip: With `unique_ptr<int[]>` the class becomes move-only automatically. Need copies? Write the deep copy, default the moves.
slides.takeaway: Rule of 0: let members own resources. The compiler-generated members then compose correctly.

text.hook:
Item's move constructor is noexcept.
The wrapper only adds an empty destructor.
That cannot change anything. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: "Why is my vector copying?" Not the missing noexcept this time.

slides.title: GCC/libstdc++. What does `reserve(3)` print?

slides.verdict_sub: Cause: the user-declared destructor removed the implicit move
bullets: Declare only a destructor: the copies are still generated, the moves are **not declared**.
So `Logged` has no move constructor. Rvalues bind to the copy constructor.
`reserve(3)` exceeds capacity 2: both elements are relocated by copy.
`~Logged() = default;` gives the same result: still user-declared.

slides.title: Default the moves
slides.tip: Simplest fix: delete the empty destructor (Rule of 0). Same output.
slides.takeaway: "Not declared" is not "deleted": rvalues silently fall back to the copy.
